Very good, OK. Ah, thank you very much, Chair Gjonaj. I want to thank you and the speaker for today's hearing on Intro 1796 and allowing me to say a few words at the outset. Um, I introduced this legislation in 2019 in response to the small businesses across the city who said that rent was the biggest challenge that they face in staying business. The numbers bear this out. Between 2007 and 2017 the commercial vacancy rate doubled across New York City. And over the last 18 months the situation has only become more dire. The push to address the small business rent price in New York City is not new, as Chair Gjonaj mentioned. In fact, New York City had commercial rent stabilization in the 1940s and 1950s in direct response to economic instability that the city was facing and the strain put on small businesses. Later in 1986 the City Council introduced legislation to regulate rent for retail spaces, citing similar hardship concerns for small businesses. Now, as our city contends with the long-lasting economic impacts of a global pandemic that hasn't been seen before in our lifetime, we are called to ask ourselves how we are committing to change. What legacy will this administration and council leave behind for our small businesses and how will we start forward on a path for a just recovery that puts the well-being of our neighborhoods first and includes the spaces that make them so unique. Local government has the ability to do big things and today's hearing of Intro 1796 shows that. But first I'd like to be clear what this bill does not do. It does not cancel rent and it does not reduce rent. It does not guarantee any business a right to a space. It does not guarantee a right to renewal of a lease. It does not interfere with existing leases or contracts. This is what the bill does. First, Intro 1796 would create a level playing field for businesses by establish a commercial rent guidelines board, much like the residential rent guidelines board, that will annually set the maximum percentage that rents for smaller commercial spaces can be increased. It will not be a decrease. There will be a setting the maximum percentage that can be increased from the existing rent paid. The bill applies universally to all commercial spaces under a certain square footage, removing the negative incentive that landlords have to push out local businesses and wait for the highest bidder, sometimes causing years of vacant storefronts. The interest to displace a local business is taken away because the next tenant would follow the same rental amount. New York City knows how rent stabilization works. It has given millions of households the security and stability that they needed to start a family and to be able to stay in the city. Small businesses deserve that same stability. Rent stabilization gives small businesses a fairer shot. Chain businesses and corporations have had a leg up in our city for years because it is currently in the landlord's fiscal interest to rent to well-capitalized businesses, making it harder for new businesses to get started. This goes against the interest of vibrant sustainable communities. Second, the rent guidelines board will be able to choose each year whether it will set rent increases, rent increase limits by setting one rate for the entire city or by identifying smaller affected areas. The board will be required to factor in things like building operating costs, neighborhood displacement, local economic impact, and vacancy rates, providing flexibility in a tailored approach to different needs across the city rather than a one-size-fits-all. The bill also brings us a step closer to standardized leases so that all commercial tenants know what to expect in their rental agreements. I have seen in working on this bill wildly fluctuating leases that have snuck in unexpected costs, sometimes not until years three or four, when a tenant was least expecting it. Clearer leases are especially important coming out of the pandemic when economic instability can lead to desperation and exploitation of those most vulnerable. And so this bill eliminates the addition of pass-alongs in leases. Your total rent will actually be your total rent. New York City has the clear legal authority to enact commercial rent regulation. There is no current state law governing commercial rent and there has not been one in generations. The city has home rule authority to regulate any area of economic life where the state does not have a regulatory scheme in place. That is why this bill is legal. Intro 1796 brings regulation stability for small businesses in a time of so much instability. It creates a system of protection and reasonable rent charge, rent, rent changes, and an end to skyrocketing rent increases and deceptive lease renewals. I want to be clear. This bill does not take aim at small landlords who are often already offering lease renewals and new leases with reasonable neighborhood market changes of 5% to 10%. It does take aim at larger corporate property holders that are gouging local businesses and causing significant displacement in our communities. Now is the time to pass this legislation, and as we start to come out of this pandemic we can offer the stability and the long-term planning that businesses have been demanding of us. Other localities are finding ways to tackle the small business rent prices. Seattle passed a law last summer to cap any commercial rent increases in response to the pandemic. When we fight for our small businesses we fight for all of us. We fight for jobs for local residents, for investment in our local economy, and the vibrancy and diversity of our neighborhoods. Our communities depend on local businesses and I'm proud to be able to put them first in this legislation. There are some folks I want to thank for this legislation. Ah, first, Kelly Taylor and Rob Newman, um, who worked on this legislation, ah, going back about three years at this point. Louis Holden Brown, Audrey Sun, Bill Drafter, Stephanie Jones, committee counsel. Um, I want to specifically acknowledge Elizabeth Adams, who put countless hours, um, into working through the complexity of this legislation. I just want to thank her, um, very much. Um, and all of the businesses in District 33 who helped inform this legislation, and members of the United for Small Business Coalition, who have also put in countless hours of work and advocacy. With that, I'll turn it back to you, Chair. Thank you very much for the courtesy.
